messages.content: What happened in the Nanjing massacre?

The Nanjing Massacre, also called the Rape of Nanjing, was a mass atrocity committed by Imperial Japanese troops after they captured Nanjing, then China’s capital, on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War.

Over roughly six weeks, Japanese soldiers killed large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed prisoners of war. They also carried out widespread rape, torture, looting, and arson. Estimates of the death toll vary because records were incomplete and definitions differ, but historians commonly place it in the range of tens of thousands to more than 200,000; the Chinese government’s official memorial figure is 300,000.

Some foreign residents and missionaries established the Nanking Safety Zone, which sheltered many civilians and documented abuses through diaries, photographs, and reports. After World War II, Japanese military leaders were tried for war crimes connected to the massacre.

The event remains a major source of grief and political tension in East Asia, particularly because some Japanese nationalist figures have minimized or denied its scale despite extensive historical evidence.

What happened in the Nanjing massacre?

The Nanjing Massacre, also called the Rape of Nanjing, was a series of mass atrocities committed by the Imperial Japanese Army after it captured Nanjing, then China’s capital, on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War.

Over roughly six weeks, Japanese troops murdered large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers, carried out widespread rape and sexual violence, looted homes and businesses, and burned parts of the city. Many prisoners of war and civilians were executed in mass killings; others died through torture, abuse, or deprivation.

The precise death toll is disputed because records are incomplete and estimates use different geographic and time boundaries. Major historical accounts and postwar tribunals have generally placed the number of deaths in the hundreds of thousands; China officially commemorates 300,000 victims. The atrocities themselves are extensively documented through survivor testimony, contemporary foreign witnesses, photographs, diaries, military records, and burial records.

The massacre remains a major source of grief and political tension in East Asia, particularly because some Japanese nationalist figures have minimized or denied aspects of it, despite the broad historical consensus that large-scale atrocities occurred.
